protocol.instrument_name: NSW Community Pharmacist Protocol: Supply of Oral Contraceptive Pill
protocol.instrument_version: Approved by Susan Pearce AM, NSW Health Secretary, 05 June 2026
protocol.legal_basis: Clause 48B of the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation 2008: a pharmacist may supply the oral contraceptive pill to a person otherwise than on prescription if the pharmacist has obtained a Graduate Certificate of Advanced Practice and Prescribing for Pharmacists from James Cook University, the supply is made in accordance with a protocol issued by the Health Secretary and published on the Ministry of Health's website, and the pharmacist keeps a record of the details of the supply in accordance with the protocol and clause 176 of the Regulation. This protocol is the approved protocol under clause 48B.
protocol.supervision_model: approved pharmacist (document's own term) — a pharmacist who has obtained a Graduate Certificate of Advanced Practice and Prescribing for Pharmacists from James Cook University; approved pharmacists must register their intent to provide the service with NSW Health, maintain up-to-date service availability listings via Healthdirect Australia, satisfy themselves they have appropriate currency of skills, identify and manage conflicts of interest, and practice within their scope of competence
protocol.scope_summary: NSW protocol for approved pharmacists to initiate, continue and change supply of oral contraceptive pills in eligible low-risk patients under clause 48B: approved medicines (Table 1 combined oral contraceptive pills, triphasic and progestogen-only pills), general requirements, adverse-event reporting, patient assessment flowchart (pages 5-6, image not extractable), key points and clinical principles, informed consent, patient assessment (history, examination, sexual and reproductive health counselling, pregnancy exclusion, contraindications), consultation room requirements, clinical documentation, resources and references. Supply limited to 3 months initially and up to 12 months subsequently, at private (non-PBS) cost.

inclusion.text: Supply is limited to clearly defined low-risk patients only; supply is restricted to patients who are assessed by the approved pharmacist as low risk.

G. PATIENT ASSESSMENT

diagnosis_pathways.name: Patient assessment flowchart and clinical pathway for supply of the oral contraceptive pill (sections D, E, F, G)

steps.description: Obtain informed clinical and financial consent prior to providing care under this protocol: ensure the patient has been provided with sufficient information about the nature and purpose of the service, the OCP options available and the rationale for the proposed supply, expected benefits and limitations of the OCP, material risks/adverse effects/contraindications, alternative options for contraception including referral, and costs (private non-PBS supply; PBS Safety Net does not apply); confirm the patient has had the opportunity to ask questions and that these have been answered to the patient's satisfaction. Informed consent for supply must be documented in the clinical record. For NSW Health pilot consultations, patients must complete the approved screening questionnaire and consent form prior to the consultation; participation is voluntary and patients may withdraw consent at any time without affecting their care.

gates.criterion: Informed clinical and financial consent obtained from the patient prior to providing care under this protocol
Approved screening questionnaire and consent form completed prior to the consultation (NSW Health pilot requirement)

provenance.section_heading: F. PATIENT CONSENT

steps.description: Take a patient history tailored to the patient's presentation (prompts are not exhaustive; maintain an open mind and be aware of cognitive bias): age; pregnancy and breastfeeding status; underlying medical conditions including new or recently diagnosed conditions assessed against UKMEC 3 and 4 (e.g. migraine with aura — patients with a UKMEC category 3 or 4 condition are not eligible for continuation and require a referral); current medications including adherence and satisfaction with any hormonal contraception (establish whether use of hormonal contraception has been continuous and provide continuation according to the protocol; if a patient frequently takes pill breaks, use professional judgement and consider referring to explore alternative contraception options e.g. long-acting reversible contraception (LARCs)); drug allergies/adverse effects; prior use of contraceptives, tolerability and adverse effects; smoking status including vaping (increased risk of combined hormonal contraception in smokers over 35 years or those who have quit smoking over the last year; footnote: vaping with nicotine is considered equivalent to cigarette smoking for MEC, and any vaping in those aged 35 years and older will be MEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception); any unexplained and un-investigated vaginal bleeding or acute, severe menstrual bleeding; any headaches indicative of migraines; last cervical screening test (HPV test) including whether the patient is up to date with screening, and breast check; HPV vaccination status. Review My Health Record where appropriate and available.

gates.criterion: Patient assessment produces no uncertainty about eligibility or appropriate management (otherwise supply must not occur and the patient must be referred)

provenance.section_heading: PATIENT HISTORY

steps.description: Consider taking a brief sexual history to inform shared decision making and assess the appropriateness of hormonal contraception continuation (previous use and experiences with contraception, current relationship status, and risk factors for STIs, including any known STI history of current and/or recent partner). Assess STI risk as part of the consultation — recommended for anyone who is sexually active and engaging in unprotected sex, has a new partner since their last STI test, or thinks they may be at risk — advise patients on appropriate testing and recommend STI testing for individuals who may be at risk even if they report no symptoms. Provide sexual health promotion advice about condoms. Guidance: https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexual-history/. Consider the STI Testing Guideline for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People for priority populations.

gates.criterion: No symptoms suggestive of STI present (presence of symptoms must result in immediate referral for medical assessment)

provenance.section_heading: Sexually transmitted infection (STI) assessment and referral

steps.description: Measure blood pressure (BP) for all patients, and the patient's height and weight to calculate BMI to determine the patient's suitability for oral contraceptive pill, and record this information in the clinical software program. A single elevated BP reading is not enough to classify an individual as hypertensive (activity immediately prior to consultation should also be taken into consideration) and a second BP reading should be taken at the end of the consultation. If BP remains elevated, the patient should be referred to a medical practitioner or health service for further assessment and selection of an appropriate contraceptive method. BP should be monitored and recorded every 12 months. BMI should be calculated on the first presentation, and professional judgement exercised regarding whether BMI needs to be recalculated on subsequent presentations.

gates.criterion: Blood pressure not elevated on the second reading taken at the end of the consultation

provenance.section_heading: EXAMINATION

steps.description: Exclude pregnancy: pregnancy must be confidently excluded prior to initiation; otherwise the patient should be referred to a medical practitioner (or other authorised prescribing health practitioner) for assessment, pregnancy testing, and advice regarding ongoing contraception. If appropriate, a discussion around emergency contraception and supply should occur. Note that pregnancy tests can give a false negative result if unprotected sex was less than 21 days earlier; false negative pregnancy tests are possible in early pregnancy and any uncertainty should trigger a referral to the patient's GP. If pregnancy cannot be confidently excluded, supply must not occur. A 'quick start' OCP initiation approach is not permitted under this protocol.

gates.criterion: Pregnancy confidently excluded prior to initiation

provenance.section_heading: Excluding pregnancy

steps.description: Confirm no UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC) category 3 or 4 conditions are present; patients with a UKMEC category 3 or 4 condition are not eligible for continuation and require a referral. Approved pharmacists must consult the referenced resources (Therapeutic Guidelines - Contraception; RANZCOG and CoSRH, previously FSRH, documentation including CoSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, FSRH Guideline Combined Hormonal Contraception, FSRH Clinical Guideline: Progestogen-only Pills, FSRH Progestogen-only Injectable Contraception, RANZCOG Contraception Clinical Guideline) and remain up to date with revisions; in addition, approved pharmacists must apply NSW protocol restrictions, including low-risk requirement and pregnancy exclusion criteria. [UKMEC 3/4 non-eligibility wording printed at page 10 PATIENT HISTORY; resource consultation requirement printed at page 15 CONTRAINDICATIONS TO HORMONAL CONTRACEPTION.]

gates.criterion: No UKMEC category 3 or 4 conditions are present

provenance.section_heading: Clinical principles

steps.description: Confirm supply is restricted to a patient assessed as low risk and that all protocol requirements are met: only formulations listed in the protocol are supplied, supply is for the primary purpose of contraception, and the patient is physically present in the pharmacy. Nothing in this protocol replaces clinical judgment; approved pharmacists must practice within their scope of competence and must follow this protocol. Where there is any uncertainty regarding patient assessment, eligibility, or appropriate management, supply must not occur and the patient must be referred to an appropriate medical or nurse practitioner or appropriate health service. Patients with a complex medical history, contraceptive needs beyond oral methods, or uncertain eligibility must be referred. Approved pharmacists must only supply therapy where they are confident in their clinical proficiency, assessment, and decision-making; where this threshold is not met, referral is required.

gates.criterion: Patient assessed as low risk and all protocol requirements met (listed formulation, primary purpose contraception, patient physically present, no clinical uncertainty)

provenance.section_heading: Clinical principles

steps.description: Supply an approved oral contraceptive pill from Table 1 (single or combined oral forms of ethinylestradiol, levonorgestrel, norethisterone, drospirenone, nomegestrol, desogestrel, dienogest, gestodene; Table 1 also lists estradiol/nomegestrol, estetrol/drospirenone, triphasic ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel formulations and progestogen-only pills). Approved pharmacists may supply up to 3-months of therapy for initial supply, including initiation or change of therapy, to ensure timely clinical review; subsequent supply may be provided for up to 12-months in accordance with this protocol and patient eligibility criteria. Choice of Approved Medicines must prioritise the lowest effective oestrogen dose and be individualised to patient risk. Supply is at private (non-PBS) cost; PBS subsidies and the Safety Net will not apply. Correct supply requires exclusion of pregnancy and identification of contraindications — incorrect supply carries a risk of serious adverse outcomes, including unintended pregnancy and avoidable harm from inappropriate exposure to hormones.

gates.criterion: All preceding assessment steps passed (consent, history, sexual/STI assessment, BP/BMI examination, pregnancy excluded, no UKMEC 3/4, low risk, protocol requirements met)

provenance.section_heading: E. KEY POINTS AND CLINICAL PRINCIPLES

steps.description: Provide comprehensive advice (including supporting written information when required) as per the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, UKMEC, and other relevant resources, including Consumer Medicines Information and/or other resources/handouts endorsed by relevant organisations. Counsel on the hormonal contraception supplied: how to take it, side effects to expect/how to manage them, when the hormonal contraceptive is less effective, what to do in the event of a missed pill, and reiterate the importance of adherence and avoiding breaks in contraceptive use to avoid risk of pregnancy. Educate patients on the importance of getting regular women's health and sexual/reproductive health checks. Discuss LARCs where appropriate as per RANZCOG recommendations (note that in some cultural groups recommendations for LARC may have overtones of reproductive coercion and this must be managed sensitively). Advise on cervical screening (routine screening available from age 25, recommended every five years), breast checks (available for all women from age 40; women actively invited from age 50; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women encouraged to commence screening at age 40; personal or family history of breast cancer — advise seeing a medical practitioner or health service), and STI screening. Be aware of local services managing domestic and family violence and local referral pathways for access to LARC.

provenance.section_heading: Provision of non-pharmacological and women's health advice

steps.description: All patients should be referred within 1 month to a general practitioner or appropriate sexual health service for: cervical screening (HPV testing); sexually transmitted infection (STI) screening; contraceptive review (including LARC discussion); ongoing preventive healthcare and risk assessment. Patients should be referred to a medical practitioner within 1 month of supply for a comprehensive sexual and reproductive health review. Patients who are not eligible must be referred to their regular medical practitioner or health service. STI testing must be supported through assessment, advice and a referral to a GP or sexual health service (within one month or earlier if clinically indicated). Cervical screening must be assessed, patients advised and supported to access appropriate screening including self-collected HPV testing where appropriate, and referred to a general practitioner or appropriate health service for testing and follow-up where indicated. Approved pharmacists must clearly communicate to the patient that pharmacist supply does not replace comprehensive medical review.

provenance.section_heading: Clinical principles

steps.description: Initial supply of up to 3 months is intended to facilitate early follow-up and clinical review; subsequent supply may be provided for up to 12-months. Make an electronic clinical record using an appropriate secure digital platform (such as MedAdvisor or Dragatron) and a record in a pharmacy dispensing system; the clinical record must provide a comprehensive outline of the consultation, patient history, assessment, clinical decision rationale, rationale for medicine selection, advice provided, follow-up plan and GP referral. Under the Regulation records must be kept for 2 years; privacy requirements generally require records to be kept for a minimum of 7 years. Where a patient has a My Health Record, ensure the details of the supply are uploaded unless requested otherwise by the patient. Share a copy of the record of the service with the patient and, if the patient consents, with the patient's usual treating medical practitioner or medical practice within a week following the consultation. For pilot consultations, record that the patient has completed the screening questionnaire and consent form. BP should be monitored and recorded every 12 months. [Record-keeping and My Health Record wording printed at pages 4, 15-16; 3-month early review wording printed at page 7.]

STI testing must be supported through assessment, advice and a referral to a GP or sexual health service (within one month or earlier if clinically indicated). (page 11)

If the patient may be at increased risk of HIV and other STIs, pharmacists should advise them to seek review from their GP or a sexual health service for further assessment, testing, and discussion of HIV and STI prevention options. (page 11)
If BP remains elevated, the patient should be referred to a medical practitioner or health service for further assessment and selection of an appropriate contraceptive method. (page 12)
refer to a general practitioner or appropriate health service for testing and follow-up where indicated (cervical screening). (page 7)
urgent: Presence of symptoms suggestive of STI must result in immediate referral for medical assessment. (page 11)

Referral options include to the local hospital, sexual health clinic and/or community-based sexual violence support services (for sexual violence/abuse identified during consultation); a list of family violence statewide support services including confidential crisis support, information and counselling in NSW is available at NSW Government domestic, family and sexual violence. (page 13)

If required, emergency contraception may be supplied as per standard pharmacy care, or the person may be referred to an appropriate medical practitioner or health service for another method of emergency contraception e.g. insertion of a copper intrauterine device. (page 13)

conditions: If the approved pharmacist becomes aware of an uncommon, unexpected or serious adverse event following treatment with an Approved Medicine, this should be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration via the usual processes, by reporting online at https://aems.tga.gov.au/ (page 4).

open_questions.topic: Patient assessment flowchart (section D) is an image and has no extractable text
open_questions.observed: Page 5 prints only 'The following guideline should be used in consultations to assess the eligibility, identity and govern supply of suitable treatments, and guide associated referral requirements.' followed by the footer; page 6 contains no text at all. The flowchart graphic itself (the D. PATIENT ASSESSMENT FLOWCHART content on pages 5-6) is not present in the text extraction.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document's central decision flowchart could not be transcribed from the text; pathway steps were therefore built from the printed prose in sections E, F and G, and the flowchart must be re-extracted from the PDF before go-live.

open_questions.topic: Table 1 rows with missing estrogen dose (merged cells) - ethinylestradiol, levonorgestrel, drospirenone, desogestrel, dienogest, gestodene, estradiol, nomegestrol, estetrol, norethisterone
open_questions.observed: Rows for drospirenone 3000 (Bella, Brooke, Rosie, Yana, Yaz), desogestrel 150 (Madeline, Marvelon), dienogest 2000 (Valette), drospirenone 3000 (Brooklynn, Isabelle, Petibelle, Rosalee, Yasmin, Yelena) and gestodene 75 (Minulet) print only the progestogen value; the estrogen dose cell is not present in the extracted text. Each sits under a section heading whose first row prints ethinylestradiol 20 [NB1] (low-dose) or ethinylestradiol 30 [NB1] (standard-dose).
open_questions.why_unclear: Two-column table layout is reflowed by text extraction; the inherited estrogen value is a merged-cell inference, not printed text, so those rows are marked confidence 'unclear'.

open_questions.topic: [NB1] and [NB2] footnote markers have no footnote text in the extraction
open_questions.observed: 'ethinylestradiol 20 [NB1]' (page 2), 'ethinylestradiol 30 [NB1]' (page 3) and 'Seasonique [NB2]' (page 3) carry markers, but no footnote definitions for NB1 or NB2 appear anywhere in the 20-page text extraction.
open_questions.why_unclear: The footnote content (which may qualify which products the marker applies to) is missing from the text; cannot be transcribed.

open_questions.topic: Seasonique row prints no dose values
open_questions.observed: Page 3 of Table 1 prints a bare line 'Seasonique [NB2]' immediately after the ethinylestradiol 30 / levonorgestrel 150 brand list, with no estrogen or progestogen values and no brand-list separation.
open_questions.why_unclear: Row is ambiguous/misaligned in extraction; recorded as its own treatment row with confidence 'unclear' rather than assuming it shares the preceding values.

open_questions.topic: Triphasic section prints Phase 1 and Phase 3 but no Phase 2
open_questions.observed: Table 1 'Triphasic: low or standard dose estrogen' extracts as 'Phase 1 (6 pills): ethinylestradiol 30 + levonorgestrel 50' and 'Phase 3 (10 pills): ethinylestradiol 30 + levonorgestrel 125' for brands Logynon ED, Trifeme, Triquilar ED. No Phase 2 row is present in the extraction.
open_questions.why_unclear: Either the Phase 2 row was not extracted or not printed; the triphasic schedule is incomplete, so the row is marked confidence 'unclear'.

open_questions.topic: Prose formulation list spelling and dose unit differ from the table
open_questions.observed: Page 2 section A prints 'a. ethinylestadiol (35 g or less)' with a stray 'μ' character extracted on the following line, while Table 1 columns print 'ethinylestradiol'. Both readings are recorded: prose 'ethinylestadiol' (page 2) and table 'ethinylestradiol' (pages 2-3); the dose reads as 35 micrograms when the stray μ is reattached, but the extracted line alone reads '35 g'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Extraction artifact and spelling discrepancy; both readings recorded rather than silently reconciled.

open_questions.topic: No numeric age bound printed in this protocol
open_questions.observed: Age appears in the history prompts ('Age') and in age-linked risk statements (smokers over 35; vaping 35+; cervical screening from 25; breast screening from 40/50), but no minimum or maximum eligibility age is stated. age_bounds therefore records nulls. The separate pilot screening questionnaire form asks 'Age (18–39)' but that is a different document.
open_questions.why_unclear: No numeric age limit is printed; cannot populate age_bounds without inventing one.

open_questions.observed: Routine referral wording appears on pages 7, 8, 11, 12 and 14; urgent wording on pages 11 and 13; the earliest referral statement is on page 7.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance object for the referral block using the first page; the range is recorded here. Individual trigger wording is separately captured in red_flags with its own page.

open_questions.topic: No numeric BP or BMI threshold printed
open_questions.observed: EXAMINATION (page 12) says a single elevated BP reading is not enough to classify an individual as hypertensive, a second BP reading should be taken at the end of the consultation, and 'If BP remains elevated, the patient should be referred'. No numeric threshold or BMI cut-off is given; BMI is calculated 'to determine the patient's suitability' with no printed value.
open_questions.why_unclear: The referral trigger cannot be structured into a numeric rule from this document; recorded as a qualitative red flag.

open_questions.observed: Eligibility requires 'no UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC) category 3 or 4 conditions', and assessment must consult Therapeutic Guidelines - Contraception and current RANZCOG/CoSRH (previously FSRH) documentation including CoSRH 'UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use' (2025). The UKMEC tables themselves are not reproduced.
open_questions.why_unclear: The engine cannot evaluate UKMEC categories without the external tables; only the printed category 3/4 rule and the migraine-with-aura example are transcribed.

open_questions.topic: Pilot questionnaire gate outcome not stated as a supply rule
open_questions.observed: 'If the patient does not complete the screening questionnaire and consent form, the consultation must not be counted as part of the NSW Health community pharmacy pilot program.' The document does not say the consultation or supply must stop; it only excludes the consultation from pilot funding counting.
open_questions.why_unclear: The on_fail for the pilot gate in PW-1-S1 is recorded as 'unclear' because the document specifies a funding/counting consequence, not a supply consequence.

open_questions.observed: 'Under the Regulation records must be kept for 2 years. However, privacy requirement generally require records to be kept for a minimum of 7 years.' (page 4); 'Records must be stored securely for minimum 2 years under the Regulation. However, records must generally be kept for a minimum of 7 years under privacy requirements.' (page 7).
open_questions.why_unclear: Both figures are printed; they are recorded together rather than reconciled, and local policy must choose the operative retention period.

open_questions.topic: Smoking/vaping rule is a stated risk, not an explicit eligibility rule
open_questions.observed: 'There is an increased risk of using combined hormonal contraception in smokers over 35 years or those who have quit smoking over the last year' (page 10) with a footnote stating vaping in those aged 35 years and older will be MEC 4 (absolutely contraindicated) for combined hormonal contraception. No explicit 'not eligible' instruction is printed for the smoking statement.
open_questions.why_unclear: Captured as exclusion EXC-11 with confidence 'unclear' and as judgement-prompt red flag RF-10 rather than asserting an ineligibility rule the document does not state; the vaping MEC 4 footnote is captured separately as EXC-10 with confidence 'medium'.

open_questions.observed: No emergency department, ambulance or 000 escalation instruction appears anywhere in the document; the most urgent printed wording is 'immediate referral for medical assessment' for symptoms suggestive of STI (page 11) and the local hospital option within sexual violence referral (page 13).
open_questions.why_unclear: Document is silent on emergency escalation; the emergency referral array is empty rather than inferred.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm handling of consent-based record sharing within one week, My Health Record upload (unless the patient requests otherwise), and the voluntary/withdrawable nature of pilot participation.
